lesson.title: Three Around a Point: The Flat Triangle Shape
lesson.summary: Trigonal planar geometry spreads three electron domains into a flat triangle 120 degrees apart, the shape behind boron trifluoride's odd stability and sulfur trioxide's perfect symmetry.
lesson.body:
When a central atom has exactly three electron domains and no lone pairs, VSEPR predicts that those three regions will spread out evenly in a single flat plane, each one 120 degrees from its neighbors. This arrangement, trigonal planar, is the geometric solution to fitting three repelling regions as far apart as possible without needing to escape into a third dimension. Because there are no lone pairs to set aside from the naming, electron geometry and molecular geometry are identical here, just as they were for linear geometry, and both are called trigonal planar.

Boron trifluoride, BF3, is the standard textbook example, and it is a particularly instructive one because boron does not follow the normal octet rule. Boron has only three valence electrons, so forming three single bonds to fluorine atoms leaves it with just six electrons around the central atom, an intentionally incomplete octet. With three bonding domains and zero lone pairs, the steric number is three, giving a trigonal planar shape with bond angles of exactly 120 degrees. Despite each individual B to F bond being quite polar, due to fluorine's high electronegativity, the molecule as a whole is nonpolar, because the symmetric 120 degree spacing causes the three bond dipoles to cancel completely.

Sulfur trioxide, SO3, provides an even cleaner illustration of the same principle applied to a molecule that does follow typical bonding patterns. Sulfur sits at the center with three equivalent bonds to oxygen atoms, distributed symmetrically through resonance, and no lone pairs remaining on sulfur. This gives three bonding domains, a steric number of three, and a trigonal planar shape with all three O to S to O angles measuring exactly 120 degrees due to the molecule's high symmetry. Like BF3, the individual S to O bond dipoles cancel by symmetry, leaving SO3 nonpolar overall.

Trigonal planar geometry also appears constantly in carbon chemistry whenever a carbon atom forms one double bond and two single bonds, a very common bonding pattern. A carbon bonded this way has three electron domains, since the double bond still counts as a single region, and no lone pairs, giving the same trigonal planar arrangement. This is the geometry around every carbon in a carbonyl group, the C double bonded to O found in aldehydes, ketones, and carboxylic acids, and it is part of why so many organic functional groups are flat, planar regions embedded within otherwise three dimensional molecules.

The transition from trigonal planar to the tetrahedral shape covered next is a useful way to see the whole VSEPR pattern taking shape: each time the steric number increases by one, the geometry must accommodate one more repelling region, and the only way to keep that new region as far as possible from all the others is to add a new dimension of spread, moving from a straight line, to a flat triangle, to a three dimensional pyramid shape built from four points instead of three.
